The "Trust?" — "Trust." scene and Lucia's line about how "in a relationship, you have to communicate" could also hint at their relationship developing gradually.

Hey Rockstar, hello my friend. How are you? I hope you're doing well. Where do you live? I hope you're living somewhere on Earth. 😄First of all, even in that giant open world, there is still so much missing. GTA VI's footage already has players pointing out many problems. Go online and look at YouTube. There are already plenty of videos about them. I'm only going to mention some: props appearing out of nowhere, invisible walls and forcefield-like collisions, limited ray tracing, characters dying before they should, 30 FPS, overly hairy arms, debris disappearing too quickly, no wind affecting balloons, bottles that seem impossible to break, solid mattresses, strange birds, enormous sparks, repeated hedges, bad backflip animations, strange water splashes, weird dollar bill physics, hairless deer, teleporting bags, low-poly cans, hair and body-detail problems, and many other little things. But forget all of that for a moment. There is something much bigger I want to talk about. Why can't we have a truly living world where ordinary people can actually live different lives? I want mining. I want excavator and heavy-equipment work. I want construction work, quarry work, stone crushing, factory jobs, garbage collection, driving garbage trucks, working on the back of garbage trucks, trucking, long-distance driving, pizza delivery, working in a bakery, delivering food to homes and businesses, and many other real jobs. I want to work hard, earn money, struggle, succeed, fail, change jobs and build a life. And I don't mean simply choosing a job from a menu. I mean actually living that job. Imagine becoming an excavator operator, working at a mine, digging earth and rock, loading trucks and working long shifts. Imagine becoming a truck driver with endless roads and destinations across a huge world. Imagine starting with nothing and eventually becoming a pilot, a commander, or even studying to become an astronaut. I want hundreds of different jobs, workplaces and people, because real life has all of these things. Every workplace should be different. You could get a good boss, good coworkers, a good teacher or a good foreman and build a peaceful life. But you could also meet cruel bosses, abusive coworkers, corrupt officials, gangs, criminals or companies that exploit workers. The player should be able to say, “I don't like this profession,” but also, “I love this profession, I just hate the people I work with.” Those are completely different things, and the game should understand that. Imagine a very kind, honest and compassionate person who has never even killed a chicken and feels terrible when an animal is killed. But life keeps pushing this person into worse situations. He works hard, does his job properly and tries to live honestly. Yet every workplace brings another problem. Maybe the boss is cruel. Maybe the coworkers humiliate him. Maybe the company refuses to pay what he is owed. Maybe he gets injured and cannot work anymore. Maybe he has to leave because he needs to join the army. Maybe he finally finds a peaceful workplace, but the pay is terrible. Maybe the boss only pretends to be kind so people will work for almost nothing. Maybe criminals control the workplace. Maybe corrupt officials protect the company. The player should have difficult choices: Submit. Bow your head, endure the humiliation, do whatever they tell you and keep your job. Fight back. Defend yourself and say, “I'm a human being too. You can't treat me like this,” knowing that you could lose your job, freedom or safety. Run. Stop going to work, leave the workplace, find another job, move to another city or even another country and start again. Sometimes running away should save you. Sometimes it should make you miss something important. Sometimes fighting back should make things worse. Sometimes it should expose the truth. You might get into a fight with your boss or foreman and accidentally kill him, forcing you to run before you are arrested. You might change your identity and leave the city or country. And because you left, you may never hear a conversation that would have revealed a huge secret. That's what I mean by a living story. You shouldn't always know why something is happening. Imagine working somewhere for years. At first your boss seems like a great person. Everyone says, “What a good boss. What a good man.” But one night, because you stayed late for your shift, you accidentally hear him talking to a powerful government official. You realize that the man everyone respects may be involved in something terrible. Maybe you don't quit because you need the money. You keep working there and slowly discover more. Another player might quit on the first day and never discover any of it. Another might fight the boss and get fired or arrested. Another might stay for seven years and discover something completely different. The player should never be forced to investigate. Imagine seeing a broken truck on the side of the road. You can stop and look at it, or simply say, “It's just a broken truck,” and drive past it. Maybe nothing happens. Maybe you never see it again. Or maybe, if you stop at the right time, on the right night, in the right year, something begins. The game should never say, “LOOK HERE! THIS IS A MYSTERY!” Let the player discover it naturally. Some mysteries should depend on your profession. A miner might discover something underground. A truck driver might pass through a place where something strange happens. A police officer might gain access to a case file. A journalist might hear information nobody else can hear. A factory worker might meet someone who knows something important. A garbage collector might find something ordinary people would never see. An astronaut might discover something completely different by leaving Earth. Every profession could be a different piece of one enormous mystery. And sometimes you shouldn't need a profession at all. You could simply be walking around the enormous map and accidentally witness something that only happens once. You might hear a conversation, see a vehicle at a certain time, follow someone without knowing why, or find something another player never sees. And the best part is that Rockstar should never tell us all of this. Don't publish a list saying, “There are 47 mysteries in GTA VI.” Let the players discover them. Imagine someone playing the game for years and then, twenty years after release, discovering something nobody else knew. He uploads it to YouTube. At first almost nobody watches it. Then one person sees it. Then another. Then another. Suddenly people start asking, “Why didn't this happen to me?” Someone says, “Because you never worked at that place.” Another says, “No, working there isn't enough. You have to hear that conversation.” Someone else says, “You have to stay for the night shift.” Then another player says, “You're all wrong. The real trigger was a choice you made seven years earlier.” 😂

If you’ve made it this far, you’ve likely witnessed life’s roller coaster come full circle at least once and survived the culminating hurricane of consumerism, waste, crime, and fraud—all byproducts of unchecked greed within the very technocratic society this game depicts.

GTA VI is, in many ways, a manifestation of where we were and where all of it has brought us, for better and for worse. I’ll play this game not to honor the deviance and chaos it portrays with shocking accuracy, but to honor those who were lost within that same reality—many of them close friends and family who loved the art of gaming, anticipated this very release, yet succumbed either directly or indirectly to the chaotic variables the game itself so vividly markets.

If you made it to November 19, then in a deeper sense, you are the real Rockstar.

We should approach this game not merely as an immersive exercise in escapism, but as a cultural pulse check—a technological mirror reflecting what we’ve become and forcing us to consider where we go next. An interactive experience this advanced is proof that we now possess tools powerful enough to begin fighting a different kind of war: one against disorder, waste, exploitation, and imbalance that doesn’t require artillery.

Perhaps the greatest value of art is not that it allows us to escape reality, but that it gives us enough distance from reality to finally recognize it.

God bless, enjoy the game, and enjoy the holidays, folks.

Good:
The game brought back the top right gun and ammo similar to San Andreas and I adore that, along with how the 5 stars looked and its amazing.
The visuals are incredible, I didnt like it at first because its so damn different to gta5 and I was used to San Andreas and GTA4 looking similar so i figured it would be the same for 5 and 6 but I hope it grows on me more tbh.
The bottom right when he interacted with the dog looked extremely similar to the controller options in Red Dead 2 with I love. And it also looks like they may have added an animal compendium like Red Dead 2 has which would be very cool and interesting to see how it works.
The combo of having switchable characters again but being able to seemingly have a relationship and spending a lot of it together is going to be incredibly nice. Obviously you can do things by yourself but going to rob a store with a partner there as the druver and stuff is amazing. As well as how she kind of hid the gun while walking into the store, that was amazing.

Bad:
Theres barely any vulgarity. I know I know "this is such a small thing it doesnt even matter blah blah" but look, gta5 was unafraid to say anything, I mean hell we got Trevor as a psychotic maniac who said the craziest thing. But for this game in the beginning with the drug dealer dudes and the hood black guys, the script sounded like they were trying to be safe with the writing. There was no N word which was partially replaced by "bruh", barely any cursing, and its just not how those people would talk at all. I've grown up around all that and it was nothing like it shouldve been.
Another negative is it didnt feel as free but I am only saying this because i didnt see any free roaming stuff which I assume is basically the same but more in depth as gta5, so this may be a non issue which I'm sure it is tbh. It's just things like the police chase looked driven by wire with direct paths. Gta5 felt free like the cops drove on their own volition but had a set path they were supposed to drive.

Jason's reload during the car chase... during a tactical reload (when the magazine is not empty yet), Jason uses the bolt release to release the bolt locked to the rear. It's a mechanical aberration: since there are bullets left, a cartridge is already in the chamber and the bolt should never lock.

The NPC in the white shirt uses a shotgun while our protagonists flee in a car, but the animation is completely empty. No shell is ejected and we don't see any cartridge being introduced.

I can't believe I’m leaving this game behind; I’ve been playing it since I was six or seven, and now I’m eighteen. I used to play it back in my old neighborhood of Zayouna, Baghdad. Later, my father’s family—my uncles and grandparents—emigrated to Germany, Sweden, and Turkey, while we stayed in Iraq and moved to the Ghazaliya district of Baghdad. That was around 2015–2016; I was seven years old and in the second grade at Al-Anwar Public School. My parents were on the verge of separating due to family issues, and we were building a new house. My mother and I were living with her family, while my father lived elsewhere due to the conflict. I played this game to find solace and escape the problems, tragedies, and harsh reality of my life. As a child, I rarely saw my father—we mostly connected through the game I played with my cousins. It was the game that shielded me from all the family tragedies and hardships. I used to play it in the room next to my grandmother’s; I owned an Xbox One back then. By 2018, I reached the stage of final exams and didn't play as much, though I still enjoyed Fortnite and GTA Online*. Yet, *GTA was the only game that stayed with me through every circumstance—sadness, happiness, depression, and tragedy. It was—and will forever remain—the one thing that comforted me and kept the sorrow at bay. I grew attached to it over thirteen years and was introduced to Arab, European, American, and Latin cultures—people from all over the world. From the enhanced version to GTA V in 2022—the best version of all—it remains the greatest. Goodbye, *GTA V*, and thank you for everything. I am proud to have played it, and now I bid it farewell. 8/30/2026

It’s funny. I think a lot of us who are here during this whole GTA VI “season” are experiencing a kind of future nostalgia without fully realizing it yet. We’re living through a moment that will eventually fade away, like everything does.

A lot of you probably started with GTA III, Vice City or San Andreas. Maybe you were a kid like I was, maybe a teenager. Back then, life was completely different. Everything felt new, everything felt bigger, and somehow everything felt a little more magical. Those graphics probably looked just as unbelievable to us back then as GTA VI looks to us now. There was always something new to discover.

And now we’re here. Older, with completely different lives, probably trying to recover a small piece of that feeling. Maybe it isn’t as strong anymore. Maybe adulthood has worn some of it away. But somehow, seeing a new GTA, watching these trailers, listening to this song and getting excited about a videogame again can still wake up that part of us that used to feel everything so intensely.

Being an adult is complicated. Life can be hard, and moments like these are finite. Some of you reading this in 2026 might not even be going through the best period of your lives. And yet, for a few minutes, all this hype might be letting you feel like that kid again. The strange part is that years from now, this exact moment will probably become a memory of its own. Maybe in three years, maybe six, maybe ten. GTA VI will already be something familiar. We’ll know every street, every character, every mission. And some of us will come back to videos like this and remember what life felt like when the game was still a mystery and everything was still ahead of us.

Maybe that memory will be happy. Maybe bittersweet. Maybe life will have changed in ways none of us can imagine right now. But I think this period will carry its own kind of nostalgia, perhaps almost as sweet as the nostalgia we have for those games from our childhood.

So, to everyone reading this in 2026: enjoy this little feeling while it’s here. Enjoy the speculation, the excitement, the waiting, the music, even the stupid arguments about trailers and graphics. Someday, strangely enough, you may miss all of it.

And to anyone finding this comment two, five or ten years from now: we were here. We were waiting for GTA VI. We had no idea what the game would become, or where life would take us by the time you read this.

For us, this was still the future.

Jason's reload during the car chase... during a tactical reload (when the magazine is not empty yet), Jason uses the bolt release to release the bolt locked to the rear. It's a mechanical aberration: since there are bullets left, a cartridge is already in the chamber and the bolt should never lock.

After all the rumors, legends, and expectations that have built up over the years, the bar for this game became so high that I was expecting to see something much better. The PC version will definitely have much, much better graphics than this.

The first two trailers had a lot more of that “wow” factor. In this gameplay trailer, I didn’t really feel the same impact.

That said, it’s also clear that there’s enormous potential here. A new game, a new adventure, a massive world, different mechanics, dozens of small realistic details that can easily go unnoticed, and plenty to discover seem to be waiting for us. So it would also be unfair to make a definitive judgment without actually playing the game.

The interplay between Jason, Lucia, and the Relationship Meter is set to be the emotional core of Grand Theft Auto VI, functioning very much like a trust and dynamic system rather than a simple loyalty bar.

1. Jason's Honor/Loyalty: Measures his personal alignment, reliability, and whether his individual choices lean toward self-preservation or sticking to the plan. If Jason's honor drops too low, he may second-guess Lucia or look for an exit strategy, leading to friction during critical heists.

2. Lucia's Honor/Loyalty: Reflects her tactical composure, street smarts, and ambition. High honor might keep her focused on long-term survival and partnership, while low or erratic honor could make her volatile, desperate, or prone to taking reckless risks that endanger them both.

3. The Relationship Meter: Acting as the bridge between the two, this measures their emotional bond, trust, and romantic or partnership stability. High trust unlocks seamless cooperative gameplay, deeper dialogue options, and unified goals. Low trust or high tension can trigger internal betrayal mechanics, arguments during missions, or completely fractured decision-making.

The combination of these three progressions will likely steer the story into distinct narrative resolutions:

1. The Bonnie & Clyde Finale (High Honor / High Trust): Both characters maintain strong individual loyalty and a high relationship meter. Despite the police closing in, they pull off the ultimate score, survive against the odds, and ride off together into the sunset—or successfully go off the grid.

2. The Split Path / Betrayal (Divergent Honor / Low Trust): If Jason's and Lucia's stats pull in opposite directions and the relationship meter shatters, the final act will likely force a brutal choice. One character may be forced to turn on the other, leading to a tragic showdown or separate escape routes where only one survives.

3. The Downfall (Low Honor / Low Trust): When both characters act purely out of self-interest and their bond is completely eroded, the partnership collapses under pressure. A botched final heist or police trap results in a bleak, uncompromising conclusion where neither makes it out clean.

Rockstar is clearly leaning into a classic neo-noir crime romance where your day-to-day choices—how you treat each other, who takes the fall, and how much you trust your partner when the heat is on—will dictate whether they beat the system or become its latest victims.

While recognising this will almost certainly be the best open world experience to date and an unprecedented level of detail, there are some simple things that frustrate me because of how easy they would be to fix.

My issues:
- 17:50 Weapon wheel and icons are basic and ugly. They would be nicer if stylised better.
- 8:48 Bushes in median island under palm trees are obviously copy pasted, they could simply rotate them slightly and solve this immersion breaking visual issue easily.
- 7:18 Jason grabs a bottle of beer from the fridge that magically appears in his hand, they could’ve easily solved this by using an animation where he grabs items from the door storage where the camera cannot see.
- 17:59 Lucia turns and her gun enters into clear sight view of cashiers but their bodies do not react at all, completely oblivious.
- 9:21 Close range gunfight yet nobody is using cover to protect themselves, unrealistic for life and death situation.
- 23:24 Jason casually walking through building not taking cover while shooting targets also not taking any cover like sitting ducks.
-24:52 Again Jason without body armour moving through a hailstorm of semi automatic gunfire unscathed and barely entering cover, casually picking off uncovered enemies one by one.
-9:12 Another close range gunfight without anyone taking cover.

Will update if I find more but it is the small details that hold the immersion together. Hopefully they are still polishing 🤞🏽

Please 🙏🏻 🥺 pay your 100 percent here rockstar and community. GTA VI looks incredible overall, but a few small details in the Extended Look stood out to me and broke the immersion a little.
• When Jason takes a bottle from the fridge, the bottle seems to appear in his hand too suddenly. A smoother hand-to-object animation would feel much more realistic.
• When Jason takes items during a store robbery, putting them inside his shirt looks a bit awkward. It would feel more believable if he used his pockets, a bag, or another visible storage method.
• Jason’s bag also seems to appear suddenly in his hand at the beginning instead of having a proper transition or pickup animation.
• Some scenes also look noticeably blurry/soft, especially when there is movement. Hopefully the final version has sharper image quality and cleaner details.
These are small things, but GTA VI is aiming for an extremely immersive world, so these little interactions make a big difference. I hope Rockstar continues polishing them before release. ❤️

Dear Rockstar Games Team,

I am writing as a long-time fan of Rockstar Games and the Grand Theft Auto series to kindly ask you to consider adding Turkish subtitles to Grand Theft Auto VI.

Turkey has a large and passionate gaming community, and the Grand Theft Auto series has been extremely popular among Turkish players for many years. Many Turkish players, including myself, have followed the series closely and greatly appreciate the incredible storytelling, characters, and attention to detail that Rockstar Games puts into its games.

For many players in Turkey, understanding English at a level sufficient to fully follow a complex story can be difficult. Turkish subtitles would make it much easier for these players to understand the dialogue, jokes, character interactions, and story details without changing the original voice acting or artistic vision of the game.

Adding Turkish subtitles would also make Grand Theft Auto VI more accessible to a significant player community and would demonstrate Rockstar Games' commitment to reaching and supporting its international audience.

I sincerely hope you will consider this request, whether at launch or through a future update.

Thank you for taking the time to listen to the Turkish gaming community. We are very excited about Grand Theft Auto VI and hope that one day we will be able to experience its story with official Turkish subtitles.

Kind regards,

A Turkish Grand Theft Auto fan

column1:
You have the right to disagree with me, that's why this is a discussion, but I would like to speak out.

I don't see any drastic differences from leaks in terms of graphics, it still reminds me of Watch_Dogs 2, especially with the poor cheap interface of the weapon selection wheel and this item selection icon. In the moments of the car chase, the game feels like the unreleased Matrix Awakening on Unreal Engine 5. The glass never broke during the entire trip, as if it was scary to show it, there are no bullet marks on the car. Fire and ignition are the very bottom, there's not even a comment. The game feels AI-like, no matter how you look at it.

Animations also look clumsy, yes, everything is fine in the cutscenes, but when you switch to gameplay, a typical GTA 5 begins in terms of body physics (especially this ridiculous animation of Jason jumping into the water with a backflip..).

The shooting was also frustrating, not even close to Max Payne 3 to this day. As for me, The Last Of Us 2 in terms of animations, Watch_Dogs 2 in terms of style and Max Payne 3 with Uncharted 4 in terms of shooting have already proved and shown everything to everyone.

But one of the worst things here is the chosen scenes to show. These are literally the latest dreary Gta online updates. Empty talk about nothing from stupid zoomers. Extremely uninteresting dialogues. The only thing I liked was the production (again in the TLOU 2 style) at the club, where Lucia was punched in the face.

There are also questions about the chosen setting. All this God-awful modernity, which only confirms the studio's desire to make more money on the project than to make it truly revolutionary. As if ordinary hard workers and office clerks could do everything they couldn't in life: here's modern America for you, have fun and pay. Actually, GTA 5 was like that too, but the era was different, more acceptable. Now they should have made the game in the same era of the 80s or even 50s, then, of course, there would be fewer complaints about the style. I even get the impression that GTA VI is a new tik-tok.. I mean, metaphorically, the same mass part of the modern world.

I would like to note that the above disadvantages do not reduce my interest in the game, it's just something that I managed to notice while watching the gameplay. I'm not saying that the game shouldn't be released or anything like that, but it definitely needs to improve.

P.S. Jason, by the way, looks too much like Arthur Morgan, but in the 21st century.

I'm going to be blunt about the things that I see that worry me based on this video and the gameplay portions. Big things that catch my eye are blatantly strong motion blur and depth of field. Often games will use these as a way to hide performance impacting things, like visual artifacts, LOD pop-in, Low resolution textures in the distance. In a few moments, like the very first scene driving a car, I notice artifacts and smearing due to temporal rendering like DLSS. Light boiling is something I also notice occasionally, it's not heavy but it's there, likely due to low resolution path tracing, which is fine in most cases but we'll see if this is gets solved later on.

Sure a game can look great, but at what cost? Where was room made in the budget for the visuals? Should I expect poor performance on even high end systems (4080 Super + Latest gen CPU combos)? These are all important questions to be asked, espcially to those propping this game up, AND those pushing the game down.

Considerably the most important questions: Will Grand Theft Auto VI be released on PC this year, or will we have to wait at least a minimum of 7 months ( GTA III ) or up to 19 months (GTA V ) for a release to show up for PC? But the vibes of GTA VI's story feel much more like GTA IV than V, taking it a bit more seriously but still is obviously a video game about organized crime. Watching It felt like watching young Aiden Pearce cosplay as Jason Duval. casual young,the mask mechanic, even the sliding animation during takedowns — it's giving Watch Dogs 1 energy. Not just this but gameplay visual elements also, camera angles, interior lighting, all of it feels lifted straight from Ubisoft's original vision.
And that's the part that stings. Watch dogs UK demo, It still holds up — over a decade later. That demo was so far ahead of its time that Rockstar, of all studios, is still drawing from it in 2026. That's not an insult to Rockstar. That's the highest compliment art can get. Artists steal from the best, and Ubisoft's own incomptence is what killed the masterpiece.
Which makes it even more tragic that Ubisoft buried their own masterpiece. The final 2014 game got visibly downgraded from that demo, partly because it had to run on outdated hardware and aging engines that couldn't keep up with what they'd promised. And that pattern never really stopped: Ubisoft has spent the last two years bleeding money, cancelling games outright, laying off staff in waves, and selling off chunks of its biggest franchises just to stay solvent. This isn't a studio that lost its magic on purpose. It's a studio that kept tripping over its own feet until the magic got left behind.
Here's the hypocrisy nobody wants to admit: when Watch Dogs got downgraded, the internet screamed "scam" for a decade straight. Fair enough — it kind of was. But the second a beloved franchise like GTA does the exact same thing — trailer hype miles ahead of what ships — suddenly it's optimized because the PS5 hardware wasn't capable of handling it — go watch Trailer 1, they said that one was shot on PS5 too.So STFU
And that's the real tragedy in all this — watching a vision that creative get strangled to death by its own studio's incompetence.It hurts man

*The Drug Run & SWAT Raid*
Jason ("Jay") and Lucia ("Lu") arrive at a local neighborhood block on an errand for a contact named Boobie to pick up a package from Raymond. Raymond is hesitant to hand over the stash due to a feud with Boobie and his partner Ernesto being missing. Moments later, Ernesto calls to warn that a law enforcement task force is en route. SWAT officers raid the building, triggering a massive shootout. While Jason and Lucia fight their way out, a gang lord named Méndez arrives, executes a street pusher, and orders his crew to clear the scene. The duo escapes the perimeter by climbing through the apartment window of an angry local resident, "Aunt Tee."

*Reconnecting with Brian*
In need of assistance and high-paying work, Jason and Lucia dress up and meet Brian (a retired former convict) and his partner Lori at a upscale bar. Brian offers them a discreet, time-sensitive job that must be executed that night. Over drinks, Brian gives Jason a warning about the volatility of their lifestyle, using a story about a runaway carousel to emphasize the importance of knowing when to get out before it crashes.

*The Getaway with Raul*
Jason and Lucia complete a vehicle delivery for a cautious contact named Raul. Upon arrival, the drop-off turns hostile as hostile forces and police converge on the location. Lucia takes the wheel, navigating tight back alleys and aggressive pursuit to successfully break line-of-sight. Impressed by Lucia's professional driving under pressure, Raul officially brings them into his operation.

*The Megamundo HQ Raid*
A broker named Val hires Jason and Lucia as security and handlers for Andrés de León, an erratic executive attending the grand opening of Megamundo's new American headquarters. While COO Petra Navarro hosts the event below, Andrés hides in a 24th-floor executive room to avoid his speech.

Midway through the event, heavily armed mercenaries storm the building and take control. Jason and Lucia fight through the corporate facility to secure Andrés, who has been captured and interrogated by gunmen demanding money. Using a grenade as a distraction, Jason rescues Andrés and neutralizes the attackers, leaving the duo reflecting on the volatile nature of their current run.

At 17:22 Jason does a backflip, but his rotational velocity does not match his flipping form. In real life, an increase in rotational velocity is due to a tuck motion, with tuck-less gainers being much slower rotationally (typically used in higher jumps). It appears from this GTA animation that you’ve modeled Jason’s form after a tuck-less gainer, however his rotational velocity is more akin to that of a tucked gainer. Before you tell me I’m nitpicking, yes, I am! It’s 2026 and this is Rockstar! The micro details matter, and I’m saying this because I care about the game.

The small (micro) stuff:
Still sliding up stairs instead of realistic stepping animations.
Weak pickup animations for weapons and bags.
Auto-aim? Please...
Magnetic rifles floating on backs? Make a sling, please.
Summoning weapons like Molotovs out of thin air, along with infinite magazines, ruins it for me.
All the micro-interactive options, like holding hands etc., are neat, however, it’s frustrating when a game nails realistic details in one area, only to ruin all that hard work with immersion breaking shortcuts in others...

As for movement: walking, running, and taking cover feel okay, but they still feel stiff in places compared to the movement in The Last of Us series. (Yes, I am aiming high, this should be the industry standard by now.) A huge open world doesn't mean much if the player character doesn't feel grounded.

Instant character swap is smooth, and the characters are genuinely likable! Shooting out of the car is solid, while shooting tires and the car damage physics are awesome.
All the things you can do in this world are great.
